1:
The verse names two audiences, and Gill and Wesley read them as two different things. "All Israel and Judah" they take to mean the people within Hezekiah's own borders — Gill has the messengers sent not only to the subjects of his kingdom but to all the Israelites dwelling in it, who had come there for the sake of religion and the worship of God, and Wesley likewise restricts the phrase to persons of the ten tribes already settled in the kingdom. The letters to Ephraim and Manasseh are then something else: an approach to all the remainder of the ten tribes, named by those two because, as Wesley explains, they lay nearest to Judah and a great many of them had from time to time joined themselves to it (2 Chronicles 15:9). Ellicott agrees on the second point and puts it flatly — Ephraim and Manasseh here stand for the northern kingdom.

Ellicott's interest is in the words themselves. The preposition rendered "sent to" he treats as a variant spelling of the usual one; the word for letters he identifies as apparently of Persian origin, cognate with terms for something written and for painting or writing, and the ancestor of the Greek term for a royal messenger. The word belongs only to late Hebrew, which is his point about the date of the writing rather than of the event. The phrase for keeping, or making, the passover unto the LORD he matches to the wording of the law itself (Exodus 12:48).

How a king of Judah could circulate a proclamation through a foreign kingdom at all is a difficulty Clarke raises before answering it twice over. It is not easy, he says, to find out how this was permitted by the king of Israel; but it is generally allowed that Hoshea, who then reigned, was one of their best kings, and the Jews hold that by this time both golden calves had been carried off by the Assyrians, the one at Dan by Tiglath-pileser and the one at Bethel by Shalmaneser. With the rival shrines gone, those who chose to worship at Jerusalem were freely permitted to do so, and Hezekiah had encouragement to issue the proclamation. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion from the regnal dates: the first year of Hezekiah was the third of Hoshea, the last king of Samaria, who is described as a better king than his predecessors (2 Kings 17:2), and doubtless therefore he did not actively oppose Hezekiah's wish for a really national passover.

Henry is alone in pressing the question of motive, and he is careful to rule out the obvious one. The invitation was sent, he insists, not with any political design to bring the revolted tribes back to the house of David, but with a pious design to bring them back to the LORD God of Israel; and he puts the distinction in Hezekiah's own mouth — let them take whom they will for their king, so they will but take him for their God. The matters in dispute between Judah and Israel, whether civil or sacred, were not to prevent any Israelite who sincerely returned to the LORD from being made as welcome at the passover as one of Hezekiah's own subjects. Henry notices what that cost the inviting party: Hezekiah shows himself passionately desirous of the prosperity of a neighbouring kingdom from which he received no toll, tribute or custom, and which had often, and not long since, been vexatious to his own. This is rendering good for evil.
2:
The decision was not the king's alone, and the body that took it is described in three ways. Gill has Hezekiah consult his nobles together with the great sanhedrim or senate of the nation. Keil and Delitzsch read the congregation in Jerusalem as the community of the capital assembled in their representatives for this very purpose. Ellicott calls them the king's grandees and the popular representatives, and renders the opening clause as a determination rather than a deliberation — the king determined, in council. He also places the sitting before the fourteenth of Nisan, so that the postponement was resolved on in advance rather than conceded after the date had slipped.

The legal warrant for a second-month passover is the same in every hand, and it is an argument from the lesser to the greater. The law allowed the feast to be kept on the fourteenth day of the second month by those whom uncleanness or absence on a distant journey had prevented from keeping it at the lawful time (Numbers 9:11). Keil and Delitzsch note that both of those reasons were present at once here, the priests being insufficiently sanctified and the people not yet gathered. What none of the commentators finds in the law is a provision for a whole nation in that case, and each of them says so in his own way. Wesley has Hezekiah reason from the proviso made for particular persons and not doubt that it might be extended to the whole congregation. Henry puts the same inference in the same terms, finding the proviso for individuals and extending it to the congregation. Clarke has the king and his counsellors think they might stretch what was granted in such individual cases to the people at large, because of the delay necessarily occasioned by the cleansing of the temple.

Clarke alone states what the alternative was, and it is this that makes the stretch look necessary rather than convenient. The purgation of the temple could not be completed until the sixteenth of Nisan, two days after the proper date, so the feast had either to be held in Ijar or adjourned a full year — and a year's adjournment, he judges, would have been fatal to the spirit of reformation which had now taken place. Henry argues the same case as a maxim: let the circumstance give way to the substance, and let the thing itself not be lost upon a nicety about the time; it is good striking while the iron is hot and taking people when they are in a good mind, for delays are dangerous.

Whether the stretch was lawful is left to the outcome by Clarke, who closes his note on the point by observing that the result showed they had not mistaken the mind of the LORD upon the subject. Ellicott adds the names of the two months and their Assyrian forms, the first being Nisan and the second Iyyar, and marks the irregularity plainly: the feast was kept not in the first month of the sacred year, as the law prescribes (Numbers 9:3), the grounds of the postponement being assigned in the verse that follows.
3:
The verse gives two reasons why the feast could not be held at the appointed time, and a third is supplied from the chapter before it. Gill names that third first: the cleansing of the temple was not finished until the sixteenth of the month, two days after the fourteenth of Nisan which the law enjoined — and besides this, he says, two other reasons follow. Ellicott fixes the moment precisely as the time when the temple had just been reopened, in the first month of Hezekiah's first year, and allows that the passover might perhaps have been held even so, had the two hindrances named here not prevented it.

The first of those hindrances turns on a single Hebrew word, and it divides the commentators sharply. The term rendered "sufficiently" occurs nowhere else. Ellicott glosses it literally as unto what was enough and takes the sense to be numerical: a sufficient number of priests had not observed the legal ceremonies of self-purification in time to hold the passover in Nisan. Keil and Delitzsch report that this numerical reading is the usual one, held by Rashi and the Vulgate and by Bertheau among the moderns, and then refuse it outright — the reference of the word to number, they say, cannot be defended. The expression denotes only sufficiency as such, and their point is that the deficiency was not merely in how many priests had sanctified themselves for the slaughtering and offering of the paschal lambs, but in the state of the priesthood generally. Wesley, so far as his note here can be read, stands with the numerical party: the priests were not in such numbers as were needed for the slaying and offering of so many thousands of paschal victims, which he infers from their having proved insufficient even for the comparatively few offerings of the previous chapter.

The second hindrance is passed over almost without comment, the people simply not having gathered themselves to Jerusalem at the legal time in the first month. Keil and Delitzsch treat it as the second of the two grounds that between them answer to the two cases the law had provided for, uncleanness and distance, so that the congregation stood in both predicaments at once.
4:
The assent is recorded briefly and read as unanimous. Gill has them all agree to it with one mind and determine that it should be done; Ellicott renders the idiom as the proposal being right in the eyes of the king, and specifies what the proposal was — to keep the passover in the second month and to invite the northern tribes, the two parts of the plan standing or falling together. What followed, on Gill's account, was a formal vote that heralds be appointed and despatched through the land so that all might know and none plead ignorance.

Two phrases in the decree are given close attention. Ellicott renders the establishing of the decree as the decreeing of a proposal, and the heralding, literally, as making a voice pass; Keil and Delitzsch accept the Vulgate's blunt "they decreed" as faithful to the sense. Both pause over the geography. The summons runs from Beersheba even to Dan, and Ellicott points out that this reverses the ancient form of the phrase, which runs from Dan to Beersheba (Judges 20:1) — the order inverted here to suit the present case, a summons issued from the south and travelling north.

The clause giving the reason for the proclamation is where the real dispute lies, and it comes down to one word. Ellicott would not render it "they had not done it of a long time in such sort as it was written" at all, but rather, not in multitude had they kept it according to the Scripture: the people had not been in the habit of coming in their numbers, and he supports that sense from the term's two later occurrences in this same chapter. Keil and Delitzsch report Rashi's construction of it the other way, as meaning that the feast had long gone unobserved by the precepts of the law, a lapse he dated from the division of the kingdom; against which they pass on Bertheau's objection, that the term is not ordinarily temporal at all.

Ellicott settles the matter by the ancient versions and then draws out its historical consequence. The Greek translators understood multitude, which he judges well done, and the Latin has it that many had not observed the feast as the law prescribed; the Syriac and Arabic, which make the clause say that their wealth had grown greatly, he dismisses with an exclamation rather than an argument. On his own construction the implication is that ever since the schism, and perhaps before it, the festival had been inadequately observed (2 Kings 23:22). He adds what the phrase "according to what is written" points back to: the statute of the feast, from which it appears the obligation bound everyone, and from the latter of the two passages he cites, probably the one in view, that Jerusalem was its only legitimate place (Deuteronomy 16:2).
6:
The men who carried the letters are identified by their function before anything else. Clarke glosses the Hebrew as the runners or couriers, persons usually employed to carry messages, and describes them in two words that between them explain why they were chosen — light of foot, and confidential. Gill marks the extent of their circuit, through both the kingdom of the ten tribes and the kingdom of the two, Judah and Benjamin. On what sort of men they were, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott differ by a degree of confidence. Keil and Delitzsch say the question cannot be determined: they may have been soldiers of the royal body-guard, or they may have been other royal couriers of the kind the later history describes. Ellicott commits himself, holding that the soldiers of the body-guard seem to have acted as royal messengers.

Ellicott's apparatus turns up two curiosities about the word in the versions. The Syriac renders it with a borrowed Latin term for letter-carriers, which the Arabic in turn misreads as "folk of Tiberias" — an error he reports with an exclamation rather than an argument. On the construction of the verse he notes that the posts went with the letters and, separately, according to the king's order, the conjunction being omitted by the Greek and Latin but kept in the Syriac. Keil and Delitzsch take the same construction and draw the practical consequence: to the written invitation of the king and his princes the runners were to add spoken words of exhortation, so that the message was carried twice over, in the letter and in the mouth of the bearer.

The appeal itself is built on a reciprocity that both of them bring out in the rendering. Turn again to the LORD, that he may turn himself to the remnant that remains to you — Keil and Delitzsch set the two turnings side by side, and Ellicott sharpens the object of the second by translating it as the survivors that are left unto you. That the word really means survivors he argues from Assyrian, comparing the verb for being alive and the noun for life.

Who those survivors had survived is answered the same way by both, and the answer dates the appeal. The kings of Assyria in the plural are Tiglath-pileser and Shalmaneser. Ellicott treats the phrase as a rhetorical reference to Tiglath-pileser's invasion of the northern kingdom and the depopulation of Galilee and Gilead, and adds that the chronicler's language may also have been coloured by recollection of the last fatal inroad, which fell in the fourth year of Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:9) — that is, after the events here narrated, which makes the phrasing the historian's rather than the herald's.
7:
The fathers and the brethren are two different sets of offenders, and the commentators separate them. Ellicott dates the fathers' guilt from the days of Jeroboam downwards, and identifies the brethren as the men of Naphtali and the land beyond Jordan whom Tiglath-pileser carried captive; Keil and Delitzsch make the brethren those carried away by Tiglath and by Shalmaneser both. Gill names the trespass concretely — worshipping the calves and neglecting the service of God in the temple at Jerusalem — and adds the Targum's gentler phrasing, that they acted deceitfully with the Word of the LORD their God. Ellicott renders the charge as unfaithfulness to the LORD and the sentence as God having made them an astonishment, which is a harder word than desolation.

The figure in the next verse is drawn out by Gill alone. To be stiffnecked is to be obstinate and refractory like heifers unaccustomed to the yoke, which draw back from it and will not submit to it. Ellicott prefers a more literal rendering of the command — harden ye not your neck like your fathers — and matches it to the verdict pronounced on the northern kingdom at its fall, that they hardened their neck like their fathers' neck (2 Kings 17:14). Henry turns the figure inward: there is in the carnal mind a stiffness, an obstinacy, an unaptness to comply with God, and we have it from our fathers — it is bred in the bone with us.

What "yield yourselves" translates is a gesture, and the meaning of the gesture is genuinely disputed. The Hebrew says give the hand to the LORD. Ellicott takes it as submission, and cites for that sense the giving of the hand to Solomon at his accession (1 Chronicles 29:24), while allowing that the phrase can also mean to make an agreement with someone (2 Kings 10:15). Keil and Delitzsch deny the submission reading for this verse specifically. The accession passage, they point out, is construed with a different preposition; here the idiom denotes the giving of the hand as a pledge of fidelity, as it does in the covenant scenes elsewhere (Ezra 10:19). Henry stands with them and presses the figure further than either: give the hand to the LORD means consent to take him for your God, and a bargain is confirmed by giving the hand — strike this bargain, subscribe with the hand to be his (Isaiah 44:5), give him your hand in token of giving him your heart, lay your hand to his plough.

Ellicott closes his note on these verses with a judgement none of the others makes, and it is about the composition of the speech rather than its content. The phrases here — entering the sanctuary, serving the LORD, the place sanctified for ever, the heat of wrath turning away — all recur in the addresses of the preceding chapters, and such resemblances, he concludes, prove the ideal character of these addresses: the words are the chronicler's framing of what was said rather than a record of it. Nobody else in the chapter treats the appeal that way; Gill, Keil and Delitzsch and Henry all read it as the message the posts actually carried.
9:
The promise is conditional, and its benefit falls on people who are not the ones addressed. Keil and Delitzsch set that out plainly: if those who remain return to the LORD, their brethren and their sons who are already in exile shall be for mercy — shall find mercy, that is, from the very men who carried them away — and for returning, which they render as a second promise, that those captives shall come again into this land. Gill, following the Targum, reads the turning itself as a return to the fear or the worship of the LORD rather than to a place.

Ellicott puts the first clause in a form that shifts where the pity sits. Not that the exiles shall find compassion, but that they shall become objects of pity before their captors, the Hebrew word standing here for that which inspires compassion rather than for the feeling itself; and he matches the construction to a psalm that says exactly this of the captivity (Psalm 106:46). On his reading the condition does not work on the captors' goodwill directly, but makes the captives pitiable in their sight.

The ground of the appeal is a formula, and two of them trace it. Gracious and merciful, in that order, Ellicott notes, is the order of the later books, where the ancient blessing has the words the other way about (Exodus 34:6); Keil and Delitzsch refer the clause to the same ancient blessing without remarking on the inversion. Ellicott also observes that the final phrase, turning aside the face, uses a different verb from the turning away of wrath in the verse before, so that the two turnings are not the same word repeated.

Clarke takes the closing promise through the Targum and finds a doctrine in it. The paraphrase he quotes has the LORD not causing his majesty to ascend up from among them if they will return to his fear, and Clarke identifies what that majesty is: the shechinah, the dwelling of the divine presence among men and the visible symbol of that presence. On this reading the thing promised is not an attitude but an abiding — the presence staying rather than withdrawing — which is a larger assurance than the verse makes on its face, and Clarke is alone in drawing it out.
10:
Why a herald out of Judah could travel through Israel unmolested is answered by Gill from the character of the reigning king. Hoshea, one of the best of their kings, did not hinder or forbid the posts, being quite willing that his people should go and worship at Jerusalem if they thought fit; and Gill draws the consequence for the hearers — they now had no excuse to make, as they had before, that their king forbade them going thither. He thinks it very probable that Hezekiah knew this, and took the freedom to send his posts on the strength of it.

That the couriers went from city to city raises a historical difficulty, and Keil and Delitzsch meet it at length. The phrase is not inconsistent with the northern kingdom having already been ruined. The Assyrians had not blotted out all the cities from the face of the land, nor carried away every last inhabitant; they had been satisfied with taking the fortresses and demolishing them wholly or in part, and had carried off only the flower of the population. Many, they add, must have escaped deportation by flight to inaccessible places, and then settled again and rebuilt in the towns and villages that had been spared or only partly destroyed once the enemy withdrew. So a land can be both conquered and still full of cities for a herald to visit.

Ellicott reads the itinerary as a mark of authenticity rather than a problem. Zebulun, which lay on the southern border of Naphtali, had itself suffered in Tiglath-pileser's invasion, and the messengers did not in fact travel north as far as Dan, though the decree had named Dan as the limit. That Zebulun and not Dan is given as the end of their journey lends an air of historical truth to the account — an invented itinerary would have matched the decree. He makes the same argument from the list of tribes that responded: Asher lay partly next to Zebulun and the rest lay south of it, the trans-Jordan tribes and Naphtali having been devastated, so that the account is self-consistent. He notes too that Ephraim and Issachar appear later among those who came, though not in this list.

The mockery is caught by both of them in the tense of the verbs. Ellicott renders it literally — they were laughing at them, and making mock of them — the first verb occurring here only, and observes that the forms imply what the Israelites did continually rather than once; the Latin version keeps that continuous sense. Keil and Delitzsch specify what was mocked, which was not the messengers merely but the two things they brought, the summons to return and the invitation to the feast. Wesley explains the refusal by appetite and then dates its cost: the generality of the ten tribes had by long want of meat lost their taste for God's ordinances, and about six years after refusing this offer of grace they were all carried away captive.

Against that, the exception is recorded without being enlarged. Gill reads the humbling of the men of Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun as confession of their idolatries and impieties, with sorrow and repentance for them and a willingness to obey; Ellicott glosses the word in one syllable as repented, and would render the opening more exactly as "but some men of Asher" rather than divers of Asher.
12:
The idiom in this verse normally means the opposite of what it means here, and two of them say so. For a divine hand to come upon a people ordinarily signifies chastisement — Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both cite the plague upon the cattle of Egypt for that force (Exodus 9:3) — but here, they agree, the same hand is a helping one, an influence exerted for good (Ezra 8:22). Ellicott would accordingly translate the opening not as "also in Judah" but as "moreover upon Judah was the hand of God," which preserves the weight of the expression while reversing its direction.

What that hand produced was unanimity, and each of them presses the point that the unanimity was not native to the men who showed it. Gill reads the single heart as a being made hearty and willing to a man, and ascribes it to the power and efficacy of divine grace. Wesley says God by the power of his grace inclined their hearts to an unanimous compliance with his will and the king's, and marks why the verse bothers to say so: it is given as the reason for a wonderful change wrought in men who had lately been given up to idolatry. Henry generalises from the case. They acted of one mind, and it was God who gave them that mind, for in the day of power subjects are made willing and it is he who works both the willing and the doing; whenever people show an unexpected forwardness toward good, his working is to be owned in it.

One phrase in the verse carries a claim about the decree itself, and Ellicott alone takes it up. The people did the commandment of the king and of the princes by the word of the LORD, and he treats that last clause not as a general piety but as a statement of authority: the royal order was inspired by divine word through a prophet. So understood, the second-month passover was not merely a lawful stretch of the statute reasoned out in council, as the earlier verses present it, but prophetically warranted — considerably firmer ground than the king's own argument from the proviso made for unclean individuals.

The assembly that followed is described in the same term the decree had used of its absence. Ellicott notes that the throng came together in great multitude, the very word whose sense he had argued over in the heralds' summons, where the complaint was that the people had not been in the habit of coming in their numbers. Its reappearance is the point: what was there said to be wanting is here what gets reported. Keil and Delitzsch say simply that the assembly became a great congregation, and Gill that they came out of the several tribes.
14:
The clearing of the city comes before the killing of the lamb, and the order is the point. Gill notes only that they arose before they slew and ate the passover; Keil and Delitzsch supply the purpose, that the city might be purified and sanctified for the feast, and identify what was removed as the illegal altars and incense places erected under Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28:24), thrown into the Kidron as the temple's defilements had been (2 Chronicles 29:16). Ellicott reads the first word as the altars of burnt offering Ahaz had set up in every corner of the city, and draws the conclusion the verse implies: thus the city was purified as well as the temple. Henry turns the sequence into the lesson he thinks it carries — before they kept the feast they cast out this old leaven, and the best preparation for a gospel passover is to cast away our iniquities, our spiritual idolatries.

The second word for the things destroyed is rare enough to need a note from both. Keil and Delitzsch take it as a substantive meaning places for incense-offerings, that is, altars intended for the burning of incense rather than the incense itself; Ellicott renders it literally as the incense-burners and observes that the term occurs here only.

The date is given exactly, and Gill catches what is preserved in it. They could not keep the feast in the month in which it should have been kept, for the reasons already given, but they kept it on the same day of the month on which it was always observed — the fourteenth held, though the month slipped.

Why the priests and Levites were ashamed is answered two ways. Ellicott makes it shame at their own past: they were ashamed of their former reluctance to purify themselves from the defilement contracted through their connection with illegal cults and sanctuaries during the late reign. Wesley and Henry make it shame at a comparison. Wesley has their negligence and remissness upbraided by the general forwardness of the people, and Henry fills the scene in — the priests and Levites blushed to see themselves outdone by the commonalty, the people being readier to bring sacrifices than they were to offer them, which put them upon sanctifying themselves so that the work should not stand still for want of hands. Both draw the same application: the zeal we observe in others should shame us out of our own coldness and quicken us not merely to do our duty but to do it with our might. Keil and Delitzsch describe the mechanism without assigning the cause, saying they sanctified themselves under the influence of a feeling of shame.

That the Levites are named here alongside the priests creates a difficulty with the previous chapter, and the two who notice it part company over how to handle it. At the dedication of the temple the Levites had been favourably contrasted with the priests, having sanctified themselves more zealously (2 Chronicles 29:34); here both are spoken of in the same terms. Keil and Delitzsch deny any contradiction and resolve it by distinguishing the parties in view — the earlier passage concerns the priests and Levites then present in or dwelling at Jerusalem, this one a wider body. Ellicott does not harmonise it at all. He calls it a verbal inaccuracy, apparently due to the writer's wish for concision.
16:
The standing in their place is a matter of prescribed order rather than of posture. Gill distributes it — the priests in their place and the Levites in theirs, where they were appointed to stand when sacrifice was offered. Keil and Delitzsch render the phrase as standing according to their right, meaning the prescribed arrangement; Ellicott prefers according to their order, and notes that the word for the place itself is used in this sense only in the latest books of the Hebrew canon. The appeal to the law of Moses the man of God he counts as one more of the chronicler's references back to the Pentateuchal legislation.

What happened at the altar was not the normal procedure, and all three who comment say so. The blood was sprinkled by the priests, but it came to them from the hand of the Levites, and Ellicott would render the clause exactly so — sprinkling the blood from the hand of the Levites. Keil and Delitzsch state the rule it departs from: in the case of the paschal lamb the father of the family who killed the lamb had himself to hand the blood to the priest for sprinkling upon the altar. On this occasion, Ellicott says, the Levites and not the laymen who presented the victims both slew the lambs and passed the blood up to be dashed against the altar.

Whose office the Levites were usurping is where Henry differs from the rest. He takes it that the Levites killed the passover, which should have been done by the priests only, and that they assisted beyond what the law ordinarily allowed in the other sacrifices as well, particularly those for purifying the unclean, of which there was now much occasion. Then he reports the other view without adopting it: some think it was the offerers' work and not the priests' that the Levites had charge of here, since ordinarily every man killed his own lamb, and now the Levites killed it for those under any ceremonial pollution. That second reading is the one Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both hold, so Henry's own preference stands alone against the others he himself cites.

The reason for the irregularity is stated in the next verse, and the uncleanness is traced to its sources. Gill specifies them: defilement contracted either by idolatry or through things which the ceremonial law counted unclean, and from which there had now been no time to cleanse themselves according to the law. Keil and Delitzsch read the Levites' charge as presiding over the slaying for every unclean person in order to sanctify the lambs to the LORD, and Ellicott settles what the sanctifying applies to — the lambs, which would have been ceremonially unclean had unclean hands killed them.

Ellicott alone follows the exception forward and finds that it did not remain one. At the passover of a later reign the Levites are again represented as doing this same work, but there it is not presented as a departure from rule (2 Chronicles 35:11), and the practice appears once more after the return (Ezra 6:20). The precedent of Hezekiah's passover, he concludes, would seem to have become the rule — what was licensed here by emergency hardened into the established usage.
18:
The tribes named are all northern, and that is taken to explain the uncleanness rather than excuse it — except by Clarke, who excuses it outright. Gill observes that Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar and Zebulun were all of the ten tribes, where idolatry had long prevailed. Ellicott says the failure to cleanse was natural in persons so long estranged from the legal religion of the LORD, and treats the list of names as indicating a documentary source behind the account. Clarke goes further: because these men came from countries that had been wholly devoted to idolatry, they were excusable. He adds the Targum's version of the prayer that follows, which reads as a plea for the erring — the LORD, who is good, have mercy on this people who err.

What they did is stated without softening, and Ellicott sharpens both halves of it. They ate the passover not in accordance with Scripture, which is to say in illegal fashion, being themselves unclean, when the law required unclean persons to abstain until the second month had come round (Numbers 9:6) — and this was already the second month. The word rendered "pardon" he takes as stronger than pardon: properly it means to make atonement on behalf of every one, the construction used for forgiveness being a different one. The title Hezekiah gives God, the LORD the good, occurs nowhere else, and Ellicott glosses it as kind or generous. Why the breach was allowed at all Henry explains from the pastoral risk of the alternative: they were loth to forbid such men communicating, lest they discourage new converts and send away complaining those whom they desired to send away rejoicing. He adds Grotius's inference, that ritual institutions must give way not only to a public necessity but to a public benefit.

Where the prayer begins is a textual question, and the two who raise it agree that the received division is wrong. Ellicott calls it obviously incorrect, and traces the mistake to the omission of the relative pronoun in the Hebrew between "every one" and "his heart he hath directed"; on his reconstruction the petition runs as one sentence — may the LORD the good make atonement for every one who hath directed his heart to seek the true God, albeit not according to the holy purifying. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same verdict and name the cost of the alternative. If the verse is broken where the Masoretic division breaks it, a word must be supplied and the directing of the heart must be referred to Hezekiah himself, as Aben Ezra did; both expedients they call inadmissible, and they note that the Greek and Latin versions and Kimchi, with most commentators, have given the division up. Gill is the one who preserves the reading they reject, reporting from Kimchi that Aben Ezra referred the prepared heart to Hezekiah.
19:
What the LORD then did to the people is the sharpest disagreement in the chapter, and it is a disagreement about one verb. Ellicott reads the healing as the averting of a bodily visitation: the prayer is thought of as turning aside divine wrath in the shape of disease and death, the law having threatened exactly that against those who defile the sanctuary (Leviticus 15:31), and he sets the case beside Abraham's prayer for Abimelech, where healing follows intercession in the plainest physical sense (Genesis 20:17). Keil and Delitzsch name that reading, attribute it to Bertheau, and refuse it: the people are not to be regarded as already sick or on the point of becoming so. The word is explained instead by sin being itself reckoned a spiritual disease, so that the healing is of the soul, or of the transgression. Wesley stands with them — healed means pardoned this their sin, and accepted them and their services as if they had been clean — and Henry widens it, holding that healing denotes not only forgiveness (Psalm 103:3) but comfort and peace besides.

Two of them stand back from the episode to say what it concedes. Henry takes the prayer as granting that where sincerity and fixedness of heart are present there may still be many defects, the service falling short of the purification of the sanctuary, and that such defects need pardoning grace, since omissions in duty are sins as well as omissions of duty. Wesley distinguishes the two purities the verse sets against each other, the purification required of those who came into the sanctuary and the internal purity these men are here acknowledged to have had. Ellicott's closing remark is about the writer rather than the worshippers: the prayer evinces a preference of spiritual sincerity over mere literal observance of legal prescriptions, which he finds all the more remarkable in an author whose principal aim is to foster reverence for the external ordinances and traditional customs of religion.

That the prayer was heard is recorded in the barest terms, and Gill takes the three steps the clause implies: the LORD heard it, accepted it, and granted what was desired. Ellicott gathers further places where healing is used of uncleanness rather than of sickness, so that the usage he argues from is not confined to this verse.
21:
The seven days are the statutory ones, and Gill says only what the law required: the feast of unleavened bread always followed the passover. What fills the verse instead is the music, and the division of labour behind it is agreed. Keil and Delitzsch assign the strings to the Levites and the trumpets to the priests, both sets accompanying the psalmody; Ellicott divides it identically, allotting the Levites their stringed instruments and the priests their clarions. He also corrects the tense and strikes a word: the verb means they were praising, continuously, right through the festival, and the "singing" of the English stands in no Hebrew original.

The phrase rendered "with loud instruments unto the LORD" is the crux, and it is odd enough that both of them stop over it. Keil and Delitzsch translate it word for word as instruments of power to the LORD and then unpack what that could mean: those by which power was ascribed to him, or, put more plainly, which were played to the praise of his might. Ellicott reaches the same construction by his own road — instruments of strength to the LORD, apparently those by which strength was attributed to him, and so those that carried the psalms — supporting it from the many songs that glorify the strength of the God of Israel (Psalm 29:1).

Having built that case, Ellicott then argues partly against it. Something is to be said, he allows, for the older English version after all, and his reason comes from the author's habits rather than from grammar: elsewhere in these books the chronicler shows a marked taste for music that was loud and strong, so "loud instruments" may be exactly his intention. He leaves the matter undecided between them, which makes him the only commentator here entertaining both at once.

Henry is not interested in the phrase and takes the fact. They sang psalms every day, priests and Levites blessing the LORD day by day with voice and instrument together, so uttering their own gladness in God and thankfulness to him while kindling one another's; and he draws the use he thinks the verse exists for — that praise should be much of our work when we assemble.
22:
The king's speech is an idiom before it is a kindness. Gill renders it as speaking to the heart of the Levites, and fills in what such words would contain — praise of their singing, exhortation to diligence, and a promise of favour and protection. Ellicott cites the prophet's comfort spoken to Jerusalem for the same phrase (Isaiah 40:2). Clarke supplies the occasion: on such festivals the priests and Levites bore great fatigue and many privations, and so needed just the encouragement this prudent and pious king gave.

What the Levites were commended for is the sharpest division in the chapter, and it turns on a single clause. Four of the voices take it as teaching. Clarke calls it a fine and expressive character given of these men, that they taught the good knowledge of God to the people, and makes it the great work of every Christian minister. Wesley reads it as their office, to instruct and build up the people in the knowledge and fear of God, and says it is named here as the very cause of the king's respect and kindness to them. Henry assigns the duty from the law (Deuteronomy 33:10) and expands it into preaching — they read and opened the Scriptures and instructed the congregation, greatly needed after so long a famine of the word — and notes that Hezekiah did not preach himself but backed those who did, lending them his countenance so that the people should respect them the more.

Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both deny that reading. The clause, they hold, is about skill in music, not in doctrine. Keil and Delitzsch set out and reject the Latin gloss making these the men more expert in divine things and able to instruct others, following Clericus instead: the phrase means those who had distinguished themselves by intelligent playing to the LORD's honour. Ellicott would render it that they were showing good skill in honour of the LORD, in their chanting and their playing, and draws the consequence for the scene — it was the musicians whom the king encouraged with kindly words of praise. On this construction the verse records a compliment on a performance rather than a tribute to a teaching ministry.

The eating is read as the congregation's and not the clergy's. Keil and Delitzsch insist the subject is not the Levites and priests merely but all who took part, and explain the odd expression — to eat the feast — as formed on the pattern of eating the passover, meaning to hold the festal sacrificial meal, which the clause about peace offerings confirms, those meals being prepared from them. Ellicott agrees that the assembly ate the meals supplied from the flesh of the peace offerings, notes the phrase is peculiar to this passage, and reports that the Greek read instead "and they finished" — a variant needing little change in the Hebrew but, he judges, against the context.

The last word of the verse is disputed in the same way as the first clause. Everywhere else in the Hebrew Bible it means to confess guilt (Leviticus 5:5), as Ellicott acknowledges, and yet here he takes it as yielding hearty thanks, an acknowledging of the divine goodness, with the Greek version on his side. Keil and Delitzsch narrow it the same way by excluding two alternatives: it denotes neither confession of sin nor, as Bertheau proposed, approaching with thank-offerings, but simply acknowledging the LORD with heart and mouth, word and deed. Henry will not choose, taking the word in four senses at once — a religious confession of their relation to God and dependence on him, a penitent confession of sins and infirmities, a thankful confession of his mercies, and a supplicatory confession of their wants — the second being precisely the sense the other two rule out.
23:
The second week is decided on by the assembly rather than imposed, though Gill has the consultation run both ways — the people took counsel among themselves and with the king and his nobles, who all agreed. Ellicott treats the verb as naming the outcome rather than the process: they determined, that being the result of taking counsel. He renders the keeping of the days literally as doing or making them, and sets the prolongation beside Solomon's lengthened dedication (2 Chronicles 7:9). Keil and Delitzsch explain the idiom the same way, to hold days being formed on the pattern of holding the passover, and note that the gladness stands as an adverbial accusative — in joy — where Ellicott adds that some Hebrew manuscripts supply the preposition.

Why the extension was possible is where Bertheau is overruled twice. Keil and Delitzsch report his view that the royal and princely gifts were rich offerings intended for further sacrificial feasts, and call it incorrect: the beasts were bestowed for the week of unleavened bread and simply proved plentiful enough for another seven days. Ellicott states the same thing without naming anyone — the gifts were so abundant that they served not only for the feast itself but for an additional week of rejoicing. On both readings the second week is a consequence of the surplus rather than its purpose, so the generosity outran the occasion it was measured for.

The verb for the giving carries more than one sense, and Gill lays three of them out. The king separated the animals from his own herds and flocks, as Kimchi takes it; or he purchased them out of his own substance at his own expense; or — as the word itself signifies — he lifted them up as heave offerings to the LORD, and then gave them to the people for thank offerings to feast upon. Ellicott settles on that third sense, rendering it as having presented them for sacrifice as a heave offering (Exodus 35:24). Wesley makes the two gifts sequential rather than alternative: first to God, to whom the appointed parts were offered in thanksgiving, and then to the people, who feasted on what remained as the offerer himself normally would — Hezekiah being the offerer and giving away his own right in the remains.

What the liberality cost is weighed by two of them in opposite directions. Wesley thinks it the more considerable for falling at the beginning of the reign, when the king found the exchequer empty and had already been at great expense cleansing and refitting the temple and preparing for the feast. Henry notes that the princes were excited by the royal example to match the bullocks and exceed the sheep, and that the effect reached beyond the week — God was honoured, the joy of the festival kept up, and the strangers encouraged to come again to Jerusalem. Then he asks what a great estate is good for except that it puts men in a capacity of doing more good, and ventures that neither king nor princes were the poorer at the year's end for it.

Two further notes attach to the end of the verse. Ellicott reads the clause about the priests literally — priests had sanctified themselves in multitude — and marks the change it records: they no longer hung back as they had earlier in this chapter and the last, so that there was now no lack of persons duly purified for the slaughter of so many victims. Henry observes what the extra week did not involve, namely any new mode of worship: they repeated and continued the old. He adds the circumstance that makes the delay costly, since the second month found them in the midst of harvest with business in the country to look after, and yet they were in no haste to return.
25:
The congregation is sorted into three classes, and Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott divide it identically. First the whole congregation of Judah together with the priests and Levites, then those who had come out of Israel, that is from the ten tribes, and last the strangers, both such as came from the northern kingdom and such as were already dwelling in Judah. Gill adds a judgement of proportion rather than of kind, taking the companies gathered from the several cities of Judah to have been without doubt the largest, and noting why the priests and Levites are counted with them — they belonged to that kingdom and dwelt at Jerusalem, where their office lay.

Who the strangers were is specified by Clarke in terms of ritual status. They were the proselytes of the covenant, men who had embraced Judaism and submitted to circumcision; and he gives the reason the point matters here, that none but such could be permitted to eat of the passover. Ellicott, working on the word itself, corrects a confusion in another commentator's note: the term here is not the same word as the one used of the Israelites who had earlier come over to Judah, with which Lange's comment runs it together (2 Chronicles 15:9).

The joy of the following verse is given a quality as well as a degree. Gill insists it was not merely carnal, a matter of eating and drinking and making merry with one another, but spiritual, arising from the restoration of the temple service and of the feasts of the LORD.

What the comparison with Solomon's time rests on draws the same answer from Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott, and both of them get it from Bertheau, whom both quote. No festival since the dedication of the temple could be set beside this one for length, for the richness of the sacrificial gifts, for the number of participants, or for the joy that marked it (2 Chronicles 7:1). Both also note why the dedication is the right comparison for length in particular: that had run to fourteen days as well, the feast of tabernacles having followed immediately on the dedicatory feast proper.

Clarke locates the superlative somewhere else entirely. What had not happened since Solomon, on his account, is not a festival of this scale but a gathering of this composition: from Solomon's time the ten tribes had been separated from the true worship of God, and now many of them, especially out of Asher, Issachar, Ephraim, Manasseh and Zebulun, joined for the first time to keep the passover. Keil and Delitzsch, having given the Bertheau answer, concede this one too in a closing clause — since the days of Solomon all the tribes had never been united at a feast in Jerusalem.
27:
Who pronounced the blessing is a textual question before a liturgical one. The Hebrew says "the priests the Levites," and Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both defend that reading against the versions. Some Hebrew manuscripts, with the Greek, Latin and Syriac, insert an "and" to make it the priests and the Levites; Keil and Delitzsch judge that conjunction a copyist's gloss carried in from the earlier list of participants, citing an earlier chapter against it, while Ellicott renders the phrase as the Levitical priests and glosses its point — these were no irregular ministrants. Wesley reads it the same way in a line: those of the Levites who were priests also, for to them only this work belonged. Gill reports both readings, noting that the Targum supplies the conjunction, and explains why the distinction mattered — there were priests in Israel not of Levi at all, men made out of any of the people, as under Jeroboam. He then offers a reconciliation nobody else attempts: the blessing was properly the priests' business, but while they blessed, the Levites may have been singing.

What the blessing was is answered from the law. Both Ellicott and Henry refer it to the priestly form given to Moses (Numbers 6:23), and Ellicott makes its grammar the reason the next clause follows: the blessing was itself a prayer that the LORD would bless, so that a report of the prayer being heard is the natural sequel. Henry draws out its double direction — in blessing the people the priests were at once the people's mouth to God by way of prayer and God's mouth to them by way of promise — and puts the effect in a phrase: what a comfort it is to a congregation to be sent home thus crowned.

That the prayer was heard is an inference, and both of those who notice it say so and name the evidence. Keil and Delitzsch have the historian conclude it from the divine blessing that evidently rested on the festival, traceable partly in the zeal the people afterwards showed for the temple worship and partly in the deliverance of Jerusalem from Sennacherib. Ellicott names the same two, the progress of reform and the wonderful deliverance from Assyria, both related in the chapters following. The verse is thus a verdict written with hindsight, not something observed on the day.

The prayer's ascent is a figure to Clarke and a scruple to Ellicott. Clarke matches the two movements — as the smoke of their sacrifices rose to the clouds, so did their prayers and supplications and thanksgivings to the heavens — and adds the Targum's version, that the prayer came up to the dwelling-place of his holy shechinah in heaven. Ellicott notices instead what the Hebrew withholds: the holy dwelling is named and entered, but the sacred Name itself is characteristically omitted. Henry turns the direction round, holding that God said Amen to the blessing and that prayer going up to heaven in a cloud of incense comes down again to earth in showers of blessings.

Clarke alone will not end on the festival. Israel now appeared in a fair way of regaining what it had lost, and he breaks off to ask how so bright a prospect came to be beclouded. His answer is the sharpest theological claim in the chapter: men are lost not for want of holy resolutions or heavenly influences but through their own unsteadiness, failing to persevere and forgetting the necessity of continuing in prayer, so that the Holy Spirit is grieved and departs, leaving them to their own hardness. Considering the heavenly influences many receive who afterwards draw back, and the fruits they bore for a time, he calls it blasphemy to say such men never had saving grace: they had it, showed it, trifled with it, sinned against it, continued in their rebellions, and therefore are lost.
